4.1. Programming the flash
The on-board 2 MB QSPI Flash can be (re)programmed either using the Serial Wire Debug port or by the special USB Mass Storage Device mode. The simplest way to reprogram the Pico’s Flash is to use the USB mode. To do this, depower the board, then hold the BOOTSEL button down during board power-up (e.g. hold BOOTSEL down while connecting the USB). The Pico will then appear as a USB Mass Storage Device. Dragging a special ‘.uf2’ file onto the disk will write this file to the Flash and restart the Pico. The USB boot code is stored in ROM on RP2040, so can not be accidentally overwritten. VSYS is the main system ‘input voltage’ and feeds the RT6150 buck-boost SMPS, which generates a fixed 3.3 V output for the RP2040 device and its IO (and can be used to power external circuitry). 4.5. Powering Pico
The simplest way to power Pico is to plug in the micro-USB, which will power VSYS (and therefore the system) from the 5 V USB VBUS voltage, via D1 (so VSYS becomes VBUS minus the Schottky diode drop). If the USB port is the only power source, VSYS and VBUS can be safely shorted together to eliminate the Schottky diode drop (which improves efficiency and reduces ripple on VSYS). If the USB port is not going to be used, it is safe to power Pico by connecting VSYS to your preferred power source (in the range 1.8 V to 5.5 V).

2. Mechanical specification
The Raspberry Pi Pico is a single sided 51×21 mm 1 mm thick PCB with a micro-USB port overhanging the top edge and dual castellated/through-hole pins around the remaining edges. Pico is designed to be usable as a surface mount module as well as being in Dual Inline Package (DIP) type format, with the 40 main user pins on a 2.54 mm (0.1″) pitch grid with 1 mm holes and hence compatible with veroboard and breadboard. Pico also has 4× 2.1 mm (± 0.05 mm) drilled mounting holes to provide for mechanical fixing, see Figure 3.

claims.claim_text: BOOTSEL mode on the RP2040 allows the board to enter a USB bootloader state, accessible via the micro-USB port, and can be triggered by shorting TP6 low at power-up.

excerpts.excerpt:
TP6
BOOTSEL TP1, TP2 and TP3 can be used to access the USB signals instead of using the micro-USB port. TP6 can be used to drive the system into mass-storage USB programming mode (by shorting it low at power-up). Note that TP4 is not intended to be used externally, and TP5 is not really recommended to be used as it will only swing from 0 V to the LED forward voltage (and hence can only really be used as an output with special care).

4.7. USB
RP2040 has an integrated USB1.1 PHY and controller which can be used in both Device and Host mode. Pico adds the two required 27 Ω external resistors and brings this interface to a standard micro-USB port. The USB port can be used to access the USB bootloader (BOOTSEL mode) stored in the RP2040 boot ROM. It can also be used by user code, to access an external USB device or host.
4.8. Debugging
Raspberry Pi Pico brings the RP2040 Serial Wire Debug (SWD) interface to a 3 pin debug header on the lower edge of the board. To get started using the debug port see the Debugging with SWD section of Getting started with Raspberry Pi Pico-series..
Note The RP2040 chip has internal pull up resistors on the SWDIO and SWCLK pins, both nominally 60 kΩ.

excerpts.excerpt: VBUS is the 5 V input from the micro-USB port, which is fed through a Schottky diode to generate VSYS. The VBUS to VSYS diode (D1) adds flexibility by allowing power ORing of different supplies into VSYS. VSYS is the main system ‘input voltage’ and feeds the RT6150 buck-boost SMPS, which generates a fixed 3.3 V output for the RP2040 device and its IO (and can be used to power external circuitry). VSYS is R-C filtered and divided by 3 (by R5, R6 and C3 in the Pico schematic) and can be monitored on ADC channel 3. This can be used for example as a crude battery voltage monitor. The buck-boost SMPS, as its name implies, can seamlessly switch from buck to boost mode, and therefore can maintain an output voltage of 3.3 V from a wide range of input voltages, ~1.8 V to 5.5 V, which allows a lot

Note The RP2040 has an on-chip linear regulator (LDO) that powers the digital core at 1.1 V (nominal) from the 3.3 V supply, which is not shown in Figure 15.
4.5. Powering Pico
The simplest way to power Pico is to plug in the micro-USB, which will power VSYS (and therefore the system) from the 5 V USB VBUS voltage, via D1 (so VSYS becomes VBUS minus the Schottky diode drop). If the USB port is the only power source, VSYS and VBUS can be safely shorted together to eliminate the Schottky diode drop (which improves efficiency and reduces ripple on VSYS). If the USB port is not going to be used, it is safe to power Pico by connecting VSYS to your preferred power source (in the range 1.8 V to 5.5 V).

RP2040 has an integrated USB1.1 PHY and controller which can be used in both Device and Host mode. 4.1. Programming the flash
The on-board 2 MB QSPI Flash can be (re)programmed either using the Serial Wire Debug port or by the special USB Mass Storage Device mode. The simplest way to reprogram the Pico’s Flash is to use the USB mode. To do this, depower the board, then hold the BOOTSEL button down during board power-up (e.g. hold BOOTSEL down while connecting the USB). The Pico will then appear as a USB Mass Storage Device. Dragging a special ‘.uf2’ file onto the disk will write this file to the Flash and restart the Pico. The USB boot code is stored in ROM on RP2040, so can not be accidentally overwritten. questions.question: How many multi-function GPIOs does the Raspberry Pi Pico expose?
questions.answer: The Raspberry Pi Pico exposes 26 multi-function GPIOs. [1][3] Of these, 23 are digital-only and 3 (GPIO 26–28) are ADC capable, with GPIO 26–29 being able to be used as either digital GPIO or ADC inputs. [1][3]

questions.question: What is the maximum Cortex-M0+ clock frequency of the RP2040 as stated in the Pico datasheet?
questions.answer: The maximum Cortex-M0+ clock frequency of the RP2040 is 133 MHz. [1]

questions.question: How much on-board QSPI Flash does the Raspberry Pi Pico have?
questions.answer: The Raspberry Pi Pico has 2 MB of on-board QSPI Flash. [1][2][5] The on-board flash in the Raspberry Pi Pico is specified as 2 MB, as confirmed by the mention of the Winbond W25Q16JV flash chip which is a 2 MB QSPI flash. [5][15]

questions.question: What ADC resolution and sampling rate does the Pico datasheet state?
questions.answer: The Raspberry Pi Pico datasheet states that the ADC has a 12-bit resolution and a sampling rate of 500 ksps. [4]

questions.question: What are the minimum and maximum VSYS input voltages for the Raspberry Pi Pico?
questions.answer: The minimum and maximum VSYS input voltages for the Raspberry Pi Pico are 1.8 V to 5.5 V. [3][5][7] The VSYS input voltage range is specified as ~1.8 V to 5.5 V, allowing the on-board buck-boost SMPS to maintain a stable 3.3 V output for the RP2040. [3][4][7]

questions.question: How many Programmable IO (PIO) blocks and state machines does the RP2040 have?
questions.answer: The RP2040 has 2 Programmable IO (PIO) blocks and 8 state machines. [1]

questions.question: What are the Pico board dimensions and thickness?
questions.answer: The Raspberry Pi Pico board has dimensions of 51×21 mm and a thickness of 1 mm. [1]

questions.question: What does BOOTSEL mode on the RP2040 do, and which host was used for its current measurements?
questions.answer: BOOTSEL mode on the RP2040 allows the board to enter a USB bootloader state, accessible via the micro-USB port, and can be triggered by shorting TP6 low at power-up. [6][2] The host used for the current measurements of BOOTSEL mode is a Raspberry Pi 4. [1]

questions.question: How many multi-function GPIOs does Raspberry Pi Pico expose, how many programmable GPIOs does ESP32 have, and what is the difference?
questions.answer: The Raspberry Pi Pico exposes 26 multi-function GPIOs. [1][5] The ESP32 has 34 programmable GPIOs. [14][15] The difference between the Raspberry Pi Pico and ESP32 GPIOs is that the Pico exposes 26 of 30 multi-function GPIOs, while the ESP32 has 34 programmable GPIOs that can be assigned various functions including digital, analog, and capacitive touch, with more flexibility in configuration and function multiplexing. [4][14][15][12]

questions.question: Compare the Pico's ADC with the ESP32's wireless connectivity: what ADC does Pico have and what Wi-Fi/Bluetooth versions does ESP32 support?
questions.answer: The Pico has a 12-bit ADC with 3 ADC-capable GPIO pins (GPIO 26–28), which can be used as analog inputs with software selection. [2][8] The ESP32 supports Wi-Fi 802.11b/g/n and Bluetooth 4.2 (Bluetooth LE) with up to 150 Mbps data rate and up to 20.5 dBm transmitting power. [9][15][16] The ESP32 integrates two 12-bit SAR ADCs and supports measurements on 18 channels. [10]

questions.answer: The RP2040 uses a dual-core Cortex-M0+ processor running at up to 133 MHz. [8] The ESP32 uses one or two Xtensa LX6 32-bit processors running at up to 240 MHz. [12][15]

questions.question: How many UART interfaces does each board's chip provide: RP2040 (via Pico) versus ESP32?
questions.answer: The RP2040 (via Pico) provides 2 UART interfaces. [1] The ESP32 provides 3 UART interfaces. [9][10]
